## Notation and recap

- In a [Poisson regression]{.blue} model, we observe $Y_i$ independent Poisson random variables, so that
$$
Y_i \overset{\text{ind}}{\sim} \text{Poisson}(\mu_i), \qquad g(\mu_i) = \eta_i = \bm{x}_i^T \beta, \qquad i=1,\dots,n.
$$


- The [canonical link]{.orange} is $g(\cdot) = \log(\cdot)$, which implies a [multiplicative structure]{.blue} for the mean.

- Under the canonical link, the [likelihood equations]{.blue} are
$$
\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i - \mu_i)x_{ir} = 0, \qquad r=1,\dots,p.
$$
The solution therefore has a nice interpretation as a [method of moments]{.blue} estimator, in that
$$
\sum_{i=1}^n y_i x_{ir} = \sum_{i=1}^n\mathbb{E}(Y_i) x_{ir}, \qquad r=1,\dots,p.
$$

## Interpretation of the regression coefficients

- Under the [logarithmic link]{.orange}, the mean has a multiplicative structure, namely
$$
\mu_i = \exp(\bm{x}_i^T \beta) = \exp(\beta_1)^{x_{i1}} \times \cdots \times \exp(\beta_p)^{x_{ip}} = \prod_{j=1}^p \alpha_j^{x_{ij}}, \qquad \alpha_j = \exp(\beta_j).
$$

- As a result, a [unit increase]{.blue} of the $j$th covariate from $x_{ij}$ to $x_{ij} + 1$, keeping the other covariates fixed, has the following impact on the new mean, say $\mu_\text{new}$
$$
\mu_\text{new} = \alpha_1^{x_{i1}} \times \cdots \times \alpha_j^{x_{ij} + 1} \times \cdots \times \alpha_p^{x_{ip}} 
= \alpha_j \left( \alpha_1^{x_{i1}} \times \cdots \times \alpha_p^{x_{ip}} \right) 
= \alpha_j \mu_i.
$$
In other words, the regression parameters, once exponentiated, can be interpreted as [relative changes]{.orange} of the mean, namely
$$
\alpha_j - 1 = \exp(\beta_j) - 1 = \frac{\mu_\text{new} - \mu_i}{\mu_i}.
$$

:::callout-tip
The interpretation in terms of relative changes is a consequence of the [logarithmic link]{.blue} function. Therefore, the same interpretation applies whenever this link is used.
:::

## Exposure rate

- Often the expected value of a response count $Y_i$ is proportional to an index $t_i$, the [exposure]{.orange}. For instance, $t_i$ might be an amount of time and/or a population size, such as in modeling crime counts for various cities. Or, it might be a spatial area, such as in modeling counts of plant species.

- In these cases, the [sample rate]{.blue} is $Y_i / t_i$, with expected value $\mu_i / t_i$. With explanatory variables, a model for the expected rate under a [logarithmic link]{.orange} has the form
$$
\log\left(\frac{\mu_i}{t_i}\right) = \bm{x}_i^T\beta \qquad \implies \qquad \log{\mu_i} = \bm{x}_i^T\beta + \log{t_i} \qquad \implies \qquad \mu_i = t_i \exp(\bm{x}_i^T\beta).
$$

- The adjustment term $\log{t_i}$ is called an [offset]{.orange}. The fit corresponds to using $\log{t_i}$ as an [explanatory variable]{.blue} and [forcing its coefficient]{.orange} to equal $1$. In **R**, it is specified as `offset(log(t))` in the model formula.

- The mean is proportional to $t_i$, with a proportionality constant $\exp(\bm{x}_i^T\beta)$ that depends on the covariates. The quantities $\exp(\beta_j)$ are interpreted as [relative changes]{.blue} of the [rate]{.orange}.

- Whether the coefficient of $\log{t_i}$ is indeed equal to $1$ can be checked by estimating it as a free parameter, as in the `ships` case study below.

## Overdispersion

- In Poisson regression the main [assumption]{.blue} is that $Y_i \sim \text{Poisson}(\mu_i)$, implying that
$$
\text{var}(Y_i) = \mu_i,
$$
where implicitly we have set $\phi = 1$. 

- However, from the analysis of the residuals or by comparing the Pearson $X^2$ statistic with $n - p$, we may realize that the data present [overdispersion]{.orange}, namely that $\text{var}(Y_i) > \mu_i$. A [common specification]{.blue} is
$$
\text{var}(Y_i) = \textcolor{red}{\phi} \mu_i,
$$
with $\phi > 1$. In either case, the Poisson regression model is [misspecified]{.orange}. 

- The two most common solutions to overdispersion are the following: 
  (i) the use of [quasi-likelihoods]{.blue}, discussed in [Unit E](un_E.html);
  (ii) the use of another parametric distribution; a typical choice is the [negative binomial]{.orange}.

## Zero-inflation

- The frequency of [zero outcomes]{.orange} is often [larger than expected]{.orange} under a Poisson model. Since the Poisson [mode]{.orange} is $\lfloor \mu \rfloor$ (for non-integer $\mu$), a Poisson GLM is inadequate when the mean is large but the modal response is 0.

- Such data are called [zero-inflated]{.blue}: some subjects have a [structural zero]{.blue}, while the others have positive counts or [random zeros]{.blue}.

- Example: weekly gym visits. Some people never exercise (structural zero), others exercise occasionally but not in the past week (random zero).

- The two most common solutions to zero-inflation are the following: 
  (i) the [zero-inflated Poisson]{.blue} (ZIP) model, a mixture of a point mass at zero, with weight $\pi_i$, and a $\text{Poisson}(\mu_i)$, so that $\mathbb{P}(Y_i = 0) = \pi_i + (1 - \pi_i)e^{-\mu_i}$;
  (ii) [hurdle models]{.blue}, which model zero vs. nonzero outcomes and then the positive counts through a zero-truncated distribution.

# Case study: the `ships` data

## The `ships` dataset

- The `ships` dataset of the `MASS` library, analysed in @McCullagh1989 (Section 6.3.2), concerns a type of [damage]{.orange} caused by waves to the forward section of cargo ships.

- The data are grouped into $40$ cells. The variables are:
  - `type`: ship type, A to E;
  - `year`: year of construction, 1960–64, 1965–69, 1970–74, 1975–79 (coded as $60$, $65$, $70$, $75$);
  - `period`: period of operation, 1960–74 or 1975–79 (coded as $60$, $75$);
  - `service`: aggregate [months of service]{.blue};
  - `incidents`: [number of damage incidents]{.orange}.

```{r}
#| classes: styled-output
data("ships", package = "MASS")
head(ships)
```

:::callout-tip
This case study is based on the [exam of 29 April 2015](../exams/2015_04_29.html).
:::

## Ships that never sailed

- There are $6$ cells with `service` $= 0$ and therefore, necessarily, `incidents` $= 0$:

```{r}
#| classes: styled-output
ships[ships$service == 0, ]
```

- Five of them are ships built in 1975–79 that would have operated in 1960–74, which is [impossible]{.orange}.

- These cells carry [no information]{.blue}: if $t_i = 0$, then $\mu_i = t_i \exp(\bm{x}_i^T\beta) = 0$ whatever the value of $\beta$. We [remove]{.orange} them, leaving $n = 34$ cells.

```{r}
ships <- subset(ships, service > 0)
ships$year <- factor(ships$year)
ships$period <- factor(ships$period)
```

## Exploratory analysis

```{r}
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-align: center
ships$rate <- 1000 * ships$incidents / ships$service # Incidents per 1000 months of service
levels_period <- c("60" = "Operated in 1960-74", "75" = "Operated in 1975-79")

ggplot(ships, aes(x = year, y = rate, color = type, group = type)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~period, labeller = labeller(period = levels_period)) +
  scale_color_tableau(palette = "Color Blind") +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(color = "Type") +
  xlab("Year of construction") +
  ylab("Incidents per 1000 months")
```

- The `service` ranges from `r min(ships$service)` to `r format(max(ships$service), big.mark = ",")` months: the counts are not comparable, and the [rates]{.blue} must be considered instead.

- Rates tend to be higher for ships [built after 1964]{.orange} and in the [period 1975–79]{.orange}, and they vary across types. Cells with little service, mostly of types D and E, give very [noisy]{.blue} rates, often equal to zero.

## Modelling the `ships` data

- Let $Y_i$ be the number of incidents and $t_i$ the months of service of the $i$th cell. A linear model would be inappropriate: the $Y_i$ are [counts]{.blue} whose variability grows with the mean, and they depend on the [exposure]{.orange} $t_i$.

- We consider the Poisson [rate model]{.blue}
$$
Y_i \overset{\text{ind}}{\sim} \text{Poisson}(\mu_i), \qquad \log{\mu_i} = \log{t_i} + \bm{x}_i^T\beta, \qquad i = 1,\dots,34,
$$
where $\bm{x}_i$ contains the intercept and the dummy variables of `type`, `year` and `period`, so that $p = 9$.

- The [baseline]{.blue} is a ship of type A, built in 1960–64 and operated in 1960–74.

- Hence, $\exp(\bm{x}_i^T\beta) = \mu_i / t_i$ is the expected number of incidents [per month of service]{.orange}.

## The rate model

```{r}
#| classes: styled-output
fit_rate <- glm(incidents ~ type + year + period + offset(log(service)),
  family = poisson, data = ships
)
summary(fit_rate)
```

```{r}
fit_null <- update(fit_rate, . ~ 1 + offset(log(service)))
lrt_null <- deviance(fit_null) - deviance(fit_rate)
```

- The [likelihood ratio test]{.blue} against the null model gives `r round(lrt_null, 2)` on $8$ degrees of freedom: the covariates are [jointly significant]{.orange}.

## Is the offset appropriate?

- We estimate the coefficient of $\log{t_i}$ as a [free parameter]{.blue}, instead of fixing it to $1$:

```{r}
#| classes: styled-output
fit_free <- glm(incidents ~ type + year + period + log(service),
  family = poisson, data = ships
)
round(summary(fit_free)$coefficients["log(service)", 1:2], 3)
anova(fit_rate, fit_free, test = "Chisq")
```

- The estimate is close to $1$ and the likelihood ratio test does not reject $H_0$: the coefficient equals $1$. The [rate model]{.orange} is supported by the data.

## Interpretation of the coefficients

```{r}
tab_coef <- exp(cbind(coef(fit_rate), confint.default(fit_rate)))[-1, ]
colnames(tab_coef) <- c("$\\exp(\\hat{\\beta}_j)$", "Lower 95%", "Upper 95%")
knitr::kable(tab_coef, digits = 3)
```

- The estimated rate for the baseline is $1000 \exp(\hat{\beta}_1) =$ `r round(1000 * exp(coef(fit_rate)[1]), 2)` incidents per $1000$ months.

- For a ship of [type B]{.blue}, the rate is multiplied by `r round(exp(coef(fit_rate)["typeB"]), 3)`, i.e. it is `r round(100 * (1 - exp(coef(fit_rate)["typeB"])), 1)`% [lower]{.orange} than for type A, the other covariates being equal.

- In the [period 1975–79]{.blue}, the rate is `r round(100 * (exp(coef(fit_rate)["period75"]) - 1), 1)`% [higher]{.orange} than in 1960–74. Ships [built in 1965–74]{.blue} have about [twice]{.orange} the rate of those built in 1960–64.

## Goodness of fit and overdispersion

```{r}
X2 <- sum(residuals(fit_rate, type = "pearson")^2)
phi_hat <- X2 / df.residual(fit_rate)
```

- The deviance is `r round(deviance(fit_rate), 2)` on $25$ degrees of freedom (p-value `r round(pchisq(deviance(fit_rate), 25, lower.tail = FALSE), 3)`) and $X^2 =$ `r round(X2, 2)`, so that $\hat{\phi} =$ `r round(phi_hat, 2)`: there is a [moderate overdispersion]{.orange}.

- Using a [quasi-Poisson]{.blue} model ([Unit E](un_E.html)), the estimates are unchanged, while the standard errors are multiplied by $\sqrt{\hat{\phi}} =$ `r round(sqrt(phi_hat), 2)`:

```{r}
#| classes: styled-output
fit_quasi <- update(fit_rate, family = quasipoisson)
drop1(fit_quasi, test = "F")
```

- `type`, `year` and `period` remain [significant]{.blue} at the 5% level.

## Conclusions

- The number of incidents must be modeled relative to the [months of service]{.blue}: the offset $\log{t_i}$ is supported by the data.

- The incident rate depends on the [type]{.orange} of ship, its [year of construction]{.orange} and the [period of operation]{.orange}.

- There is a [moderate overdispersion]{.orange}. Accounting for it widens the confidence intervals, but the conclusions do not change.
